content.text: Gensler argues that the golden rule follows from consistency. Imagine yourself in the other person's exact place.
If you do something to them, consistency asks you to accept it being done to you there. If you would not consent to that, your actions and your attitudes clash.

examples.title: The steps
lines: I am about to do A to X.
Imagine the same act done to me, in X's exact place.
I do not consent to that.
examples.conclusion: So acting this way is inconsistent with my own attitudes.

examples.title: Keeping their needs
lines: X needs quiet to sleep. I love loud music.
In X's exact place, I would need the quiet.
examples.note: The test uses X's needs, not my tastes.

question.prompt: On this view, what does the golden rule forbid?
options: Acting toward others in a way you would not consent to in their place
question.hint: The rule is about a clash between how you act and what you would accept.
question.explanation: It forbids acting toward others in a way you would not consent to if you were in their exact place.
